subject: Environment
topic: Climate science II — tipping points — mixed tiers
description: Permafrost, albedo, ocean acidification, feedback loops

questions.stem: 'Permafrost' — ground that remains frozen for two or more consecutive years — is a major climate concern because, on melting, it releases:

options.option_text: Carbon dioxide only
Methane and carbon dioxide
Nitric acid
Sulphur dioxide

questions.explanation: Permafrost (mostly in Siberia, Alaska, northern Canada) locks up ~1.5 trillion tonnes of carbon — twice as much as currently in the atmosphere. As it thaws, microbes decompose the organic matter, releasing CO₂ aerobically and methane (CH₄) anaerobically. Methane is ~25× stronger as a GHG than CO₂ over 100 years. This is a major 'positive feedback' — warming triggers release that causes more warming.

questions.stem: The 'albedo' of a surface measures its:

options.option_text: Ability to conduct electricity
Reflectivity of incoming sunlight
Carbon storage capacity
Biological productivity

questions.explanation: Albedo = fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected back to space (0 = pure absorber; 1 = perfect mirror). Fresh snow ~0.80; sea ice ~0.50-0.70; dark ocean ~0.06; forests ~0.10-0.15. When ice melts, darker ocean is exposed — lower albedo — more absorption — more warming. This 'ice-albedo feedback' is why the Arctic warms ~4× faster than the global average.

options.option_text: Oil spills from tankers
Absorption of atmospheric CO₂ by seawater
Dumping of plastic waste
Run-off of agricultural fertilisers

questions.explanation: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid) — seawater has taken up roughly 25-30 % of human CO₂ emissions, lowering surface pH from 8.2 (pre-industrial) to ~8.1 today. Lower pH dissolves the calcium-carbonate shells of corals, pteropods and certain plankton. Fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication (oxygen depletion), a different problem. Plastic and oil are physical pollutants.

questions.stem: In the context of the IPCC Assessment Reports, 'RCP 8.5' refers to:

options.option_text: A low-emission scenario
A high-emission 'business as usual' scenario
A mitigation policy pathway
A global temperature target

questions.explanation: RCP (Representative Concentration Pathway) 8.5 — named for its radiative forcing of +8.5 W/m² by 2100 — is the highest-emission scenario in IPCC AR5 (2014). The lower pathways — RCP 6.0, 4.5, 2.6 — represent progressively deeper mitigation. AR6 (2021-22) replaced RCPs with the broader Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), combining emission pathways with socio-economic storylines.

questions.stem: Glacial retreat in the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region affects billions of downstream people chiefly through changes in:

options.option_text: Atmospheric humidity
Dry-season river flows
Solar radiation intensity
Bird migration patterns

questions.explanation: Himalayan and Karakoram glaciers feed the upper Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra — crucial for dry-season (post-monsoon, spring) flows that keep the rivers running when the monsoon is absent. As glaciers retreat, flows initially INCREASE (extra melt), then DECLINE as the ice mass shrinks — 'peak water' is expected mid-century in many basins. ~2 billion people across South Asia depend on these rivers.

options.option_text: A source that emits carbon into the atmosphere
A natural or artificial reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases
A basin where coal is mined
A storage device for fossil fuels

questions.explanation: Carbon sink — a natural or engineered reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it emits — slowing climate change. The three largest natural sinks are oceans (25-30 % of human emissions), land vegetation / soils (~25 %), and the atmosphere (~50 %, the part that stays). 'Blue carbon' sinks are coastal (mangroves, seagrass, salt marshes). India's NDC under Paris includes creating an additional ~2.5-3 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent sink through forest / tree cover by 2030.

questions.stem: The term 'tipping point' in climate change refers to:

options.option_text: The budget allocated to climate action
A threshold beyond which change becomes self-sustaining
The moment sea level exceeds high-tide mark
The election date of a climate-sceptic government

questions.explanation: A tipping point is a critical threshold where small additional forcing pushes a climate subsystem into a new state that is hard or impossible to reverse. Documented examples — Amazon rainforest die-back, Greenland / West Antarctic ice-sheet collapse, Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation shutdown, boreal forest die-off, coral-reef collapse. IPCC AR6 (2021) raised concern that several tipping points may activate at warming levels as low as 1.5-2 °C.

questions.stem: The 'thermohaline circulation,' often described as the global ocean conveyor belt, is primarily driven by density gradients caused by differences in which two properties of seawater?

options.option_text: Differences in sunlight intensity and tidal force patterns
Differences in water temperature and dissolved salt concentration
Differences in ocean floor depth and surface wave frequency
Differences in seafloor composition and prevailing wind directions

questions.explanation: Thermohaline circulation is driven by water density differences arising from temperature (thermo) and salinity (haline) — cold, salty water is denser and sinks, powering the deep global conveyor. Option A is wrong because tides and sunlight intensity drive surface mixing, not the density-driven deep circulation that defines the thermohaline system.

questions.stem: Which greenhouse gas, released in large quantities as Arctic permafrost thaws, carries a Global Warming Potential (GWP) approximately 80 times that of CO₂ over a 20-year timeframe, making it a key climate tipping concern?

options.option_text: Nitrous oxide (N₂O), emitted mainly from agricultural soil denitrification
Tropospheric ozone (O₃), produced by photochemical smog near Earth's surface
Methane (CH₄), produced by anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in wetlands
Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), released from industrial cooling and refrigeration units

questions.explanation: Methane (CH₄) has a 20-year GWP of roughly 80–85 times that of CO₂. When permafrost thaws, previously frozen organic matter decomposes anaerobically, releasing large methane pulses — a major self-reinforcing tipping risk. Nitrous oxide (N₂O) is also potent but is primarily an agricultural emission, not the dominant gas from permafrost thaw.

questions.stem: The Amazon rainforest 'dieback' tipping point describes a threshold beyond which the forest converts to savanna. Which pair of stressors is primarily responsible for pushing the Amazon toward this tipping point?

options.option_text: Rising UV radiation from stratospheric ozone loss combined with industrial acid rain
Invasive non-native species replacing native canopy trees combined with increased soil erosion
Deforestation cutting local rainfall recycling combined with climate-driven prolonged drought
River water over-extraction combined with methane emissions from Amazon cattle ranching

questions.explanation: The Amazon recycles up to half its own rainfall through evapotranspiration. Deforestation disrupts this moisture feedback, while climate warming prolongs dry seasons — together these stressors can cross a threshold where savannification becomes self-sustaining. Option A is a common distractor; UV and acid rain are not primary drivers of Amazon biome collapse.

questions.stem: The 'ice-albedo feedback' is a classic positive feedback loop in climate science. Which statement correctly explains why this feedback is classified as 'positive'?

options.option_text: Melting ice exposes dark ocean or land surfaces that absorb more solar heat, driving further warming
Polar ice reflects extra sunlight to space, creating a net beneficial cooling for the climate system
Glacial meltwater cools surrounding ocean surfaces, temporarily offsetting regional greenhouse warming
Ice stores CO₂ under high pressure, releasing it upon melting to fertilise ocean phytoplankton

questions.explanation: In climate science, 'positive' means self-amplifying, not beneficial. Melting sea ice or glaciers exposes dark ocean or soil with far lower albedo, which absorbs more solar radiation, warms the surface, melts more ice — a self-reinforcing loop. Option B describes a negative (stabilising) feedback and is the opposite of ice-albedo feedback's actual behaviour.

questions.stem: Cryosphere scientists estimate the Greenland Ice Sheet may cross an irreversible melting tipping point at approximately what level of global mean temperature rise above pre-industrial levels?

options.option_text: Around 0.5 °C above pre-industrial — a warming threshold already exceeded decades ago
Around 4–5 °C above pre-industrial, equivalent to a worst-case RCP 8.5 trajectory
Around 3 °C above pre-industrial, representing the midpoint across all IPCC scenario ranges
Around 1.5–2 °C above pre-industrial levels, per leading cryosphere research consensus

questions.explanation: Multiple studies, including IPCC AR6 assessments, estimate the Greenland Ice Sheet's irreversible tipping point at approximately 1.5–2 °C of global warming above pre-industrial levels. Beyond this, internal feedbacks sustain melting even if emissions drop sharply. Option B (4–5 °C) confuses the general RCP 8.5 end-of-century projection with the specific Greenland threshold.

questions.stem: The 'Hothouse Earth' hypothesis (Steffen et al., 2018) describes an irreversible planetary warming trajectory. Which statement BEST captures the core scientific argument of this hypothesis?

options.option_text: Rising solar luminosity alone triggers tipping cascades, rendering all CO₂ reduction efforts futile
Abrupt methane hydrate release is sufficient to cause +6 °C warming within a single decade
~2 °C of warming may activate self-reinforcing tipping cascades that sustain heating beyond human mitigation
Deep ocean heat uptake reverses abruptly past 2 °C, rapidly releasing centuries of stored thermal energy

questions.explanation: Steffen et al. (2018) argued that near ~2 °C of warming, interlinked tipping elements — permafrost thaw, Amazon dieback, ice-albedo feedbacks — could create a self-sustaining 'Tipping Cascade' pushing Earth into a permanent 'Hothouse' state even if anthropogenic emissions fall to zero. Option A is wrong because solar variability is not the mechanism; Option B overstates both the speed and the scale of methane hydrate release.

questions.stem: 'Marine Ice Sheet Instability' (MISI) is a key tipping mechanism for the West Antarctic Ice Sheet. Which physical process makes MISI inherently self-reinforcing once retreat begins?

options.option_text: Retrograde bed geometry means retreat moves the grounding line into ever-deeper water, amplifying ice discharge
Surface melt lubricates the ice bed, accelerating basal sliding of the sheet toward the open ocean
Warmer currents divert away from ice shelves, slowing basal melt and temporarily stabilising the front
Subglacial volcanic heat melts the ice base and is amplified by increasing overburden ice pressure

questions.explanation: MISI occurs because the West Antarctic bed deepens inland (retrograde slope). As the grounding line retreats, it encounters greater water depth, thickening the ice column at the margin, increasing gravitational driving stress, speeding ice flux, and accelerating calving — a self-reinforcing runaway. Option B describes basal lubrication, a distinct process relevant to outlet glacier acceleration but not the defining MISI mechanism.
